source.title: The Randomness of Input Data Spaces is an A Priori Predictor for Generalization
source.authors: Martin Briesch; D. Sobania; Franz Rothlauf

record.tranche_reason: Tests how randomized labels on natural image data relate to test error, using a label-landscape randomness measure rather than the original study’s method.
record.gate_note: The study trains on natural and progressively randomized labels, reporting test-error results in Figures 3 and 4. Precise test-error values are figure-only in the supplied text and are not reconstructed. The reported Pearson correlations measure association with the proposed randomness indicator, not versions V2–V8.
record.test_reason: The study repeats label-randomization experiments and measures training accuracy and held-out classification error, as in V1's original experiments. Its additional randomness predictor does not change that direct test. The architectures and binary tasks differ.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that random-walk label-sequence randomness measured using Maurer's universal test provides an a priori indicator of generalization error in their binary tasks. They acknowledge dependence on manifold approximation when decision variables are unknown.
record.recipe_differences: Uses binary classification, label randomization sweeps, and a random-walk randomness measure; does not reproduce the original memorization experiments or their model set.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and randomization method change the measured relationship; for input randomization, the reported effect differs between MNIST and CIFAR10.

fits_no_version.finding: The label-landscape randomness predictor correlates with held-out error: Pearson's r between error and (1-p) is below -0.97 on binary MNIST and CIFAR10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Randomness of labels encountered during neighborhood random walks predicts generalization error in the tested binary tasks.

record.problems: Precise test-error values are available only in figures; the study is restricted to binary classification, and the authors note that the neighborhood depends on an approximate manifold when decision variables are unknown.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 2, 4, and 5 also report results for synthetic tasks, input-randomization variants, and easy versus hard cats-versus-dogs samples. These are not separately extracted because the precise test-error values are figure-only and do not add a separately stated test of V1 beyond the natural-data label-randomization sweep.

untested.parts: The original multiclass CIFAR-10 and ImageNet configurations, including Inception V3's incomplete random-label fit, are not tested. Absence of explicit regularization is not documented.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison on the same image task.
No optimizer comparison or tuning-budget comparison.
No magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness or comparison with norm and margin measures.
No removal of examples selected by memorization influence followed by retraining against random-removal controls.

record.verdict_notes: The text establishes perfect training fit and a qualitative deterioration in held-out performance with label randomization. It does not establish the two chance-relative endpoints required for a definitive V1 verdict without the plotted values, so no label is assigned. This is unavailable evidence, not an observed limitation or failure of V1. Figures 2, 4 and 5 are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the named small Inception, AlexNet, or MLP configurations on CIFAR-10 with fully random labels as specified; tests binary MNIST and CIFAR10 with label randomization and different architectures.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.size_stated: two hidden layers with 4,096 neurons each
rows.stage_stated: trained with Adam until convergence to 100% accuracy on the train data
rows.operation_detail: Trained on binary MNIST with labels randomized at probability v; test error plotted across randomization levels.

conditions.value: probability v; levels not stated in text

rows.note: The text says generalization error has a strong correlation with the randomness measure; precise plotted test-error values and the natural-versus-random-label comparison are not stated.
rows.check: The architecture and training setup are correct. Section 3 reports 100% training accuracy, and Section 3.2 reports increasing generalization error with label randomization. However, the supplied Figure 3 contains no readable plotted values establishing natural-label performance far above chance or fully randomized-label performance at chance. Randomization applies to both training and test labels; the baseline is binary random guessing.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.size_stated: three convolutional layers with 32/64/64 filters of kernel size 3x3, followed by a dense layer with 256 hidden neurons
rows.stage_stated: trained with Adam until convergence to 100% accuracy on the train data
rows.operation_detail: Trained on binary CIFAR10 with labels randomized at probability v; test error plotted across randomization levels.

conditions.value: probability v; levels not stated in text

rows.note: The text reports Pearson’s r below −0.97 between test error and the randomness measure; it does not state precise test-error values.
rows.check: The architecture and training setup are correct. Section 3 reports 100% training accuracy, and Section 3.2 reports increasing generalization error with label randomization. The reported correlation below -0.97 concerns the randomness predictor, not distance from chance. Figure 3's endpoint errors cannot be read from the supplied text. Randomization applies to both training and test labels; the baseline is binary random guessing.
